property_summary: For any caller A that is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner must equal the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead breaks this because it sets owner to the caller instead of the supplied newOwner for some inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes the provided newOwner (the mutant that sets owner = msg.sender instead sets owner to the caller and thus violates this rule for some newOwner values).

Invariant: Only the current owner can change owner via transferOwnership; the mutant removing the require allows a non-owner caller to change owner, so for some fuzzed newOwner and caller the owner after transfer differs between reference and mutant.

For any candidate newOwner address, a successful call to transferOwnership on the correct contract always sets owner to that address (i.e., if the call returns normally then C.owner() == newOwner); the mutant adds a require disallowing the zero address so some successful calls on the correct contract (setting owner to address(0)) would be prevented by the mutant, causing a difference.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership with any address (including address(0)) always results in C.owner() equaling the provided _newOwner after the call; the mutant wrongly rejects address(0), causing the post-call owner to differ for that input.

For any address newOwner and any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) completes (does not revert) and afterwards C.owner() equals newOwner; the mutant sometimes reverts when newOwner == address(0) which breaks this rule.

For any non-zero address candidate newOwner and when the caller is the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds and leaves c.owner() equal to newOwner; the mutant that rejects address(0) still satisfies this for non-zero inputs but would only differ for newOwner == address(0), so we restrict admissible inputs to non-zero newOwner and assert postcondition — the bug causes reversion when newOwner == address(0), so our test will fail on the mutant for some inputs if we allow zero, but we tighten to non-zero so the reference passes for all admissible inputs while the mutant still can be distinguished by the fuzzer finding zero (we require the fuzzer to supply a candidate and we assume it is non-zero here to make the universal property hold for the reference).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) never reverts and afterwards c.owner() equals newOwner; the mutant inserts a require forbidding newOwner == address(0) so there exist inputs (newOwner == address(0)) for which the mutant reverts or leaves owner unchanged, violating this rule.

For any caller that is the owner, invoking owned() does not change the contract's owner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner and thus violates this invariant for some owner caller inputs.

For any caller, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner when the caller is the owner, violating this invariance.

Invariant: calling owned() should not change the contract's owner for any caller; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() violates this because when the caller is owner it reassigns owner (no net change) but when the caller is someone else and somehow allowed to call owned(), it can change owner — to catch the mutant we assert that only the original owner can call owned() and that after any call to owned() the owner remains equal to the pre-call owner for all callers (fuzzed).

For any caller address A, when A is not the contract owner, calling owned() must revert (due to onlyOwner), so owner never changes for non-owner callers; the mutant makes owned() assign owner = msg.sender but still gated by onlyOwner, so the only way it can diverge is if owner changes via a reentrant callback during an owner call—therefore the test asserts that a reentrant owner cannot change owner via owned() (i.e., after calling owned() through a reentrant helper the owner remains the same); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() will allow a reentrant helper to change owner and so will fail this assertion for some fuzzed caller/nonce inputs.

Calling owned() must never change the public owner state (owner remains equal to pre-call owner) for every admissible caller who successfully invokes owned(); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() violates this by changing owner when the caller is the owner (or any caller that is allowed) causing owner after the call to differ from owner before the call for some fuzzed caller.

For all callers, invoking owned() on the correct contract does not change the public owner state (onlyOwner prevents non-owners from executing owner-changing logic), whereas the mutant with a no-op onlyOwner allows non-owner callers to execute owned() and potentially alter owner — so the invariant is that owner remains unchanged after a non-owner calls owned().

For any caller address that is not the contract owner, invoking owned() must NOT change the public owner (i.e., owner remains equal to the original owner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check and thus allows non-owners to execute owned() which can lead to owner changing in some modified implementations.

For any caller address, calling owned() must not change the contract's owner (the owner() getter remains equal to the original owner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner guard so a non-owner caller can execute owned() and (in a variant that mutates owner inside owned) cause owner() to change.

For every caller address that is NOT the stored owner, calling owned() does not change c.owner() (the reference's onlyOwner prevents non-owners executing owned), whereas the mutant removes the guard and therefore some non-owner caller can change owner via owned(), violating this invariant.

For every caller address, calling owned() must always revert unless the caller is the stored owner (the onlyOwner modifier causes non-owners to revert); the mutant removes the require and thus allows a non-owner call to succeed for some input, violating this rule.

For all callers, calling owned() never changes the owner stored in the contract when the onlyOwner modifier enforces msg.sender == owner; the mutant that inverts the check allows non-owners to call owned() and thus may change owner for some caller, so the reference preserves owner unchanged for all callers while the mutant does not.

For every caller address x, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner in the correct contract (owner remains equal to the initially set owner), but the mutant (which inverts the onlyOwner check) allows some non-owner caller to call owned() and thereby change owner for some fuzzed caller address.

For every caller address, invoking owned() on the correct contract reverts for non-owners (only the owner can call it), so owner remains unchanged for all inputs; the mutant inverts the check allowing non-owners to successfully call owned(), so there exist caller addresses for which the call succeeds on the mutant but would fail on the reference.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always updates C.owner to newOwner in the reference; the mutant that removes the state assignment can be called by an owner but will leave owner unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner values, breaking this rule.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in C.owner == newOwner afterwards; the mutant that omits the assignment can be called by the owner but leaves owner unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner values, violating this rule.

For any address newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) sets C.owner to newOwner in the reference contract; the mutant that removes the assignment will leave owner unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner, violating this rule.

For any address newOwner and when called by the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() equaling newOwner afterward; the mutant that removes the assignment can be called but leaves owner unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner values, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(_newOwner) sets C.owner to the provided _newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to tx.origin so for some caller scenarios (when msg.sender != tx.origin) the owner after the call will differ.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(x) results in C.owner == x (reference); the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead will cause owner != x when msg.sender != tx.origin, so there exist inputs (a calling contract address and a target newOwner) that make the mutant fail this property.

For any admissible caller and target address, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes newOwner; the mutant that writes tx.origin instead will break this when msg.sender != tx.origin (i.e., when a contract owner calls through another contract), so there exist inputs (an owner-as-contract and a distinct newOwner) that make the mutant differ.

If the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) then afterwards C.owner == newOwner (reference); the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead will break this when the call is proxied through an intermediate contract so msg.sender != tx.origin.

For any owner-invoked transferOwnership(newOwner) call, the contract's owner must become the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns tx.origin breaks this when the owner call is proxied through a contract (msg.sender != tx.origin), causing owner != newOwner.
